# Features

> Persistent terminal sessions, parallel coding agents, Git worktrees, diffs, an integrated editor, CLI automation, and read-only MCP access in Paneflow.

Canonical: https://paneflow.dev/docs/features

<!-- Auto-generated mirror of paneflow.dev - do not edit by hand.
     Source of truth: the paneflow.dev docs. Regenerated by
     scripts/sync-public-docs.ts in the site repo. -->

Paneflow is a native terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Built with
Rust and GPUI, it brings parallel agents, persistent terminal sessions,
Git worktrees, diffs, and an integrated editor into one interface. Run your
usual CLI tools, follow their progress, and take over when needed.

New to Paneflow? Start with [Get started](/docs), then use this page as the
feature map.

## Feature map

- **Workspace:** panes, layouts, projects, tabs, and session restore.
  Read [Layouts](/docs/layouts).
- **Agents:** agent panes, project threads, free chats, and lifecycle status.
  Read [Conductor](/docs/conductor).
- **Context:** file tree, branch badges, dev-server ports, and clickable URLs.
  Read [Shortcuts and actions](/docs/keybindings).
- **Orchestration:** CLI, JSON-RPC IPC, `paneflow up`, `paneflow flow`, and
  event streams. Read [Scripting](/docs/scripting).
- **MCP:** read-only pane access for configured agents. Read
  [Scripting](/docs/scripting).
- **Changes and Files:** a dock beside the active tab with the checkout's diff
  against `HEAD`, including untracked files, and an integrated code editor.
- **Settings:** themes, terminal defaults, workspace templates, and AI access
  controls. Read [Settings](/docs/settings).

## Workspace model

Paneflow organizes **workspaces**, **tabs**, **panes**, and **surfaces**.
A workspace groups a project's tabs. Each tab contains a pane layout, and a
pane can hold terminal or Markdown surfaces. Several coding agents can run in
the same tab. A tab can use the existing checkout or a separate Git worktree;
creating a new branch or worktree is optional.

Split the focused pane horizontally (`Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+D`) or vertically
(`Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+E`). Each new pane starts a shell in the same working
directory. Move focus with `Alt+Arrow`, open another workspace with
`Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+N`, and reshape the current pane tree with the four
[layout presets](/docs/layouts): even horizontal, even vertical, main
vertical, and tiled.

Session restore saves the workspace layout, pane tree, working directories,
custom buttons, projects, and chats. Terminals run in an independent local
host process. Choose **Keep sessions running** when quitting Paneflow to leave shells
and agents running; reopening the app reconnects to those sessions with their
screens restored. This keeps sessions alive across closing the interface,
not a machine restart or host crash. Choosing to stop sessions on quit ends
their processes.

Closing a pane, tab, or workspace stops the sessions it contains. To remove a
pane from the layout while keeping its process alive, use **Hide from Layout**
in the pane menu. Hidden sessions remain in the sidebar and reopen with one
click.

A shell or command that exits, with any exit code, leaves its pane in place as
a read-only view of its final output: typing `exit` no longer closes the pane,
so close it like any other. The host keeps up to 512 KiB of an ended session's
final screen and scrollback, and reopening the session from the sidebar shows
that text. Nothing restarts on its own: restoring a layout or opening an ended
session attaches to it, and the pane bar offers **Restart** when you want a new
process. Sessions that no open workspace claims are listed once under
**Other sessions** in the sidebar.

Restart opens a new shell; resuming an agent conversation is a separate action.

Closing a tab shows a toast with an **Undo** button, and `Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+T`
reopens the most recently closed tab or pane with its split layout, working
directories, scrollback, names, and font sizes; the terminals come back as new
shells. `Cmd/Ctrl+Alt+S` moves keyboard focus to the Workspaces sidebar, where
the arrow keys, Home, and End move, Enter opens, Space folds, F2 renames,
Delete closes a tab, Alt+Up and Alt+Down reorder, and Escape returns to the
pane.

## Agent supervision

Launch Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Pi, Hermes, or any CLI agent that
is available on your `PATH`. Paneflow runs the agent in a normal PTY pane, so
you can watch the raw terminal, interrupt it, or take over with the keyboard.

Claude Code and Codex report lifecycle state (thinking, needs input, finished,
errored) through hooks. That state lives in a worker, `paneflow serve`, that
runs detached, one per Paneflow home directory, and outlives the window like
the terminal host does: it reduces the hooks to one state per session,
rebuilds that state from disk when it restarts, and decides which desktop
notifications fire. A "finished" notification fires only for a turn that
completed, never for a failure, an interrupt, or an exit. `paneflow sessions`
prints the list the sidebar shows without a window, and `--follow` prints each
transition.

Install the hooks once per machine: click **Install hooks** on the agent's row
in **Settings > Agents**, or run `paneflow integrations install claude-code` or
`paneflow integrations install codex`. Codex asks you once to trust the new
hooks with `/hooks`. The same command registers the Paneflow MCP bridge and, for
Claude Code, the conductor skill. An entry that another Paneflow home owns (a
debug build next to a release, or a second `PANEFLOW_HOME`) is left alone: the
command names both homes, and `--force` takes the entry over. The hooks exit immediately outside a Paneflow pane. Other
CLI agents still run in panes, but Paneflow only knows what it can infer from
the process tree and terminal activity.

Inside a project, use project threads for independent agent sessions scoped to
the codebase. For research, planning, or quick questions outside a project,
open an agent chat from your home directory (`~`). Past chats stay reachable
from the sidebar.

## Workspace context

Open a repository as a workspace and organize its work in tabs. Branch
information and the file tree follow the active checkout. Switch between
workspaces in the sidebar and between tabs within a project while keeping
each pane's local context.

The file tree lets you browse the current workspace, open a file next to an
agent session, and copy absolute or relative paths for prompts and commands.
Custom action buttons let you pin frequent commands such as build, test, lint,
or dev-server starts to the top of the window.

When a process inside a pane binds a listening port, Paneflow attributes the
port to that pane from the OS process and socket tables on Linux, macOS, and
Windows. Known frontend tools such as Next.js, Vite, Nuxt, Remix, Astro,
Webpack, Angular, and React scripts can surface clickable URLs. Terminal banner
matching adds labels for more server types when output contains enough signal.

## Scripting and MCP

The `paneflow` binary is also a local CLI over Paneflow's JSON-RPC IPC socket.
Scripts can list panes, read scrollback, search output, inspect agent state,
stream lifecycle events, split panes, focus panes, prefill prompts behind a
write gate, spawn declarative workspaces with `paneflow up`, and run
multi-agent DAGs with `paneflow flow`.

Flow files define the steps and their dependencies explicitly. The runner
coordinates those steps; code review is performed by the agent or command you
run. Prompt submission and other mutations require the relevant explicit
permissions.

Paneflow also ships a read-only MCP bridge. Once installed for a supported
agent, it exposes `list_panes`, `read_pane`, and `search_pane` so an assistant
can inspect another pane without copy-paste. The bridge cannot type into panes
or control them, and terminal output is returned as untrusted data.

The full command reference lives in [Scripting and automation](/docs/scripting).

## Worktrees

Create Git worktrees for independent tasks without touching your main checkout.
Paneflow opens each worktree as its own context with its own branch, files,
panes, and agent sessions. This makes parallel agent work visible without
collapsing every task into the same working tree.

Read the [Worktrees](/docs/worktrees) page for how worktrees are created,
stored, cleaned up, and restored.
